children: By Tanner Brown
China's shoppers have found an unusual way to get their money's worth: paying a supermarket for permission to shop.

An annual membership at Walmart's Sam's Club costs 260 yuan, about $37. The chain had 10.7 million paying members in China as of June, and its brisk expansion looks almost out of place in an economy whose consumers have grown increasingly reluctant to open their wallets.

Elsewhere, the numbers are grim. Sales at stores devoted to a single brand fell 10.3% in the first nine months of 2026, while department-store sales declined 2.9%, according to government figures released Monday. Supermarkets and convenience stores managed gains of 4.1% and 5.2%, respectively.

Warehouse membership stores, meanwhile, posted growth exceeding 25% through August, according to the China National Commercial Information Center. Overall Chinese retail sales rose just 1.1% in the first nine months.

The figures don't prove that shoppers have abandoned famous labels. A pair of sneakers bought online doesn't ring up at a brand-exclusive store. But they suggest that where Chinese consumers shop — and whom they trust to deliver value — is changing.

Consider Walmart and Nike. Walmart's China revenue rose 20.7% in its latest reported quarter, to $7 billion, excluding currency fluctuations. New clubs helped, but comparable sales, which strip out much of the effect of expansion, also climbed 9.7%. E-commerce sales jumped 26% and accounted for 55% of China sales. Sam's Club was a major contributor.

Nike is heading the opposite direction. Its Greater China revenue plunged 26% in its latest quarter on a currency-neutral basis, its ninth consecutive quarterly decline there. Digital sales through its own channels fell 28%, and its physical-store sales dropped 14%.

Yet Nike's troubles aren't universal. Rival Adidas reported a 15% increase in Greater China sales in its second quarter, also excluding currency fluctuations. China's Anta Sports grew first-half revenue 12.9% across its global portfolio of brands. Chinese shoppers clearly haven't stopped buying sportswear. They're becoming more selective about which brands get their money.
Nike is trying to respond. Beginning in January, the company plans to concentrate Chinese online sales in official storefronts and its own channels, phasing out most partner-operated shops.
"When the experience is consistent, the brand becomes stronger," Cathy Sparks, Nike's Greater China chief, wrote in a post on the company's website.

The comparison between Nike and Walmart has limits: One sells discretionary apparel, the other plenty of groceries and household essentials. The lesson isn't that supermarkets have discovered a cure for weak spending. It's that brand recognition alone is no guarantee of growth.

For years, international companies could charge hefty premiums in China through name recognition, celebrity endorsements and prestigious storefronts. After a prolonged property slump and years of shaky consumer confidence, shoppers have more reason to ask what those premiums actually buy.

Consumer-market analyst Tang Jiansheng pointed to down jackets sold at Sam's Club and other supermarkets as evidence of changing attitudes toward labels and quality. He cited a 499-yuan Sam's Club jacket that sold out at multiple stores.
"Consumers are no longer buying a particular clothing brand, but the retailer's ability to select products and its promise of quality," he said.

That's Sam's pitch: a limited assortment of products it has already vetted, including private-label groceries and household goods, alongside competitive prices and speedy delivery. Customers pay for the idea that somebody has done the comparison shopping for them. Once they have paid, they have another reason to return.

In an October survey by Chinese research firm iiMedia, 51.2% of respondents cited access to carefully selected merchandise as a reason to shop at warehouse clubs. That helps explain the appeal of Costco, too. Its private-label products invite shoppers to trust the retailer's judgment rather than a manufacturer's logo.

But trust is expensive to maintain. In June, China's market regulator summoned Walmart executives over recurring food-safety problems at Sam's Club. Rapid expansion has placed new demands on a business built around screening its suppliers and products.

Yuan Shuai, an analyst with Zhongjing Media Think Tank, argues that the membership model relies on confidence in product quality. "Once that foundation of trust is shaken, even the fastest expansion is just a castle in the air," he said.

For investors, the winners won't necessarily be the cheapest retailers or the companies with the flashiest names. Walmart's China growth also comes with the costs of opening clubs, making deliveries and keeping prices attractive. Strong sales aren't the same as strong profits.
The irony is that Walmart may be winning China's contest for consumer loyalty by asking shoppers to pay for it in advance.
